lessons.title: کہنا (kahnā) — to say
lessons.gloss: to say — the verb beside بولنا that carries the words themselves, and four letters the reader can already write

segments.source: [PAUSE 2s]

segments.text: Chapter six taught bolnā, "to speak" — a word whose opening letter is still ahead of you in the script ladder, so it stays in romanization here. Urdu has a second verb here, and the line between them is the line between the act and the words.

segments.instruction: the complementiser two lessons back — ki
segments.source: [YOU RECALL: the complementiser two lessons back — *ki*]

segments.text: کہنا — kahnā — to say, to tell.
Four letters, all of them yours: ک، ہ، ن، ا. Strip the -نا of chapter six and the stem is کہ-.

bolnā is about producing speech — maiṅ urdū boltā hūṅ, I speak Urdu. کہنا (kahnā) is about the content — what somebody actually said. English merges the two under speak and say without a clean rule; Urdu keeps them apart, and after کہنا (kahnā) the clause introduced by کہ follows naturally.

کہنا (kahnā) is Sanskrit kathayati, "to tell, to relate," on the noun kathā, "a story." That noun is still in Urdu as کہانی, kahānī, "a tale" — the word a chapter-seventeen writing lesson already put in front of you. To say and a story are one root, two syllables apart.

Its stem کہ- looks exactly like the borrowed complementiser کہ of the last chapter and has nothing to do with it: one is inherited from Sanskrit, the other borrowed from Persian, and they collided on the page. Urdu is full of these seams.

lessons.title: کیا کہا؟ (kyā kahā?) — what did you say?
lessons.gloss: what did you say? — the repair sentence a beginner reaches for second, made of two words this book has now taught and nothing else

segments.source: [PAUSE 2s]

segments.text: Chapter nineteen gave you the first thing a lost learner says. This is the second, and it is made of the verb from the lesson before and one word from chapter three.

segments.instruction: the sentence chapter one deferred — maiṅ nahīṅ samajhtā
segments.source: [YOU RECALL: the sentence chapter one deferred — *maiṅ nahīṅ samajhtā*]

blocks.title: You'll want to know: کیا کہا؟

segments.text: کیا کہا؟ — kyā kahā? — what did you say?

Two words. کیا is the what of chapter three, back in the middle of the sentence where it means what rather than marking a yes-or-no question — the distinction the nineteenth chapter drew. کہا is کہنا (kahnā) in the past, the form you use for something that has already been said.
Say it with the voice rising and it is a request to repeat. Said flatly, with a frown, it is a challenge — so the tune matters more here than in any sentence this book has taught.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the repair kit, in three sentences

utterances: when: you did not follow at all. say: maiṅ nahīṅ samajhtā.
when: you did not catch the words. say: kyā kahā?
when: you want it slower. say: the next lesson.

segments.text: Not one of these needed a new word before this chapter. کیا has been in the book since chapter three, نہیں since chapter one, and کہنا (kahnā) arrived one lesson ago. What was missing was somebody putting them next to each other.

lessons.title: آرام سے (ārām se) — slowly, gently
lessons.gloss: slowly, gently, take it easy — the third piece of a beginner's repair kit, and five letters already yours

segments.source: [PAUSE 2s]

segments.text: Asking somebody to say it again only helps if they say it again at a speed you can follow.

segments.instruction: the request from the lesson before — kyā kahā?
segments.source: [YOU RECALL: the request from the lesson before — *kyā kahā?*]

blocks.title: You'll want to know: آرام سے

segments.text: آرام سے — ārām se — slowly; gently; take your time.
آرام سے کہیں — ārām se kaheṅ — please say it slowly.

The wave over the first letter is the alif madda of chapter seven. سے is the postposition with, so the phrase is literally with ease — and the second word is the same سے the book has been showing since chapter three in āp se mil kar.

آرام is Persian ārām, "rest, ease, repose," on an old Indo-Iranian root for standing still. So Urdu's way of asking somebody to slow down does not ask them to be slow; it asks them to be at ease. That is a gentler thing to say to a stranger than the English request, and it is why ārām se also means take it easy, carefully, and no rush depending on where it lands.
کہیں is کہنا (kahnā) in the polite request form. You are not asked to learn that ending here — only to hear that the verb from the last lesson is inside it.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the repair kit is now whole

when: you want it slower. say: ārām se kaheṅ.

segments.text: Three sentences, four chapters, and not one new letter. Before chapter nineteen this track had no repair language at all: a learner who lost the thread had شکریہ and نہیں and nothing else.

segments.text: Four chapters ago this book could not deny a sentence, ask a yes-or-no question, join two nouns, give a reason, or say that it had not understood. Say the sentence chapter one promised and never delivered. (maiṅ nahīṅ samajhtā.) Say the question that asks for a repeat. (کیا کہا؟ (kyā kahā?)) And say the four members of the k- family. (kyā, kahāṅ, kyūṅ, kaun.)
